prayer.text: Saint Peter Chrysologus, pray for us.

cues.text: A Deacon Elevated
Peter was born in Imola, in the Roman province of Aemilia, in the last years of the fourth century — ancient sources vary on the exact date, some placing his birth around 380, others closer to 400.
The local bishop, Cornelius, baptized him, educated him, and in time ordained him deacon, forming the plain, direct preaching style that would later make him famous.
Around 433, Pope Sixtus III consecrated Peter bishop of Ravenna, then serving as the seat of the Western Roman emperors.
Apparently, this set aside the candidate the Ravennese clergy and people had themselves elected, a highly unusual intervention.
Later biographers explained it, though without contemporary confirmation, by a vision guiding the pope's hand.
Whatever moved the choice, Ravenna received in its new archbishop a preacher of rare discipline just as the Western Empire, in its final decades, most needed steady pastoral leadership.
The Golden-Worded

The name Chrysologus, 'golden word,' was almost certainly bestowed on Peter in his own century, likely by the imperial court, in deliberate echo of the great Eastern preacher St. John Chrysostom, whose name meant the same.
Peter earned it not through length but economy: his surviving sermons, some 176 collected in later centuries, run only a few minutes each.
He told his congregation plainly that he kept them short out of respect for their attention rather than any shortage of things to say.
With the backing of empress-regent Galla Placidia, who governed in the name of her young son Valentinian III, Peter built and adorned churches across Ravenna.

He worked steadily to root out the last vestiges of pagan practice among his people, cautioning them in surviving sermons against indecent public dancing and old superstitions dressed up as harmless custom.
A Steadying Voice in a Doctrinal Storm

In 448 the Eastern monk Eutyches was condemned by a synod at Constantinople for teaching that Christ possessed only a single, divine nature after the Incarnation — the heresy that would come to be called Monophysitism.
Eutyches, seeking allies, appealed to Peter, whose closeness to Pope St. Leo the Great and reputation for orthodoxy made him a natural figure to court.

Peter's reply survives among the acts of the Council of Chalcedon : he withheld his own judgment on the theological question and instead firmly instructed Eutyches to submit to Rome's authority and accept whatever Pope Leo determined.
It was a small act with large consequences: a bishop of no great see used his personal credibility not to build a faction of his own.
Instead, he pointed a wavering churchman back toward unity as the controversy moved toward the ecumenical council that would settle it three years later.
Death and a Quiet Homecoming
Peter died around the year 450, according to tradition at Imola, the small town of his birth, to which he had returned near the end of his life to venerate the relics of St. Cassian of Imola.
Ancient accounts, more devotional than strictly verifiable, describe him making a final offering at that shrine before he died.
Through the martyr's intercession, he commended his soul — a fittingly modest close for a bishop whose entire pastoral method had been built on brevity and humility rather than display.
Legacy
It was not until 1729, nearly thirteen centuries after his death, that Pope Benedict XIII named Peter Chrysologus a Doctor of the Church.
This recognition was astonishingly overdue for sermons their own author had insisted were too brief to matter much beyond the moment of their preaching.
He shows every preacher, and indeed every believer who has ever worried that they have too little to offer, the power of faithfulness.
Small and disciplined acts — a few unadorned minutes of teaching, a letter written to steady a wavering friend rather than to win an argument — can outlast empires built on far grander ambitions.

Ravenna's empire is gone; the golden-worded bishop's plain, short sermons on prayer, fasting, and mercy are still read, not least his own most quoted words: 'Fasting is the soul of prayer, almsgiving is the lifeblood of fasting.'
